verses.zh: 申初祷告的时候，彼得、约翰上圣殿去。
verses.en: Now Peter and John were going up to the temple at the time[NOTE:1] for prayer,[NOTE:2] at three o’clock in the afternoon.[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “hour.”

Going up to the temple at the time for prayer. The earliest Christians, being of Jewish roots, were still participating in the institutions of Judaism at this point. Their faith in Christ did not make them non-Jewish in their practices.
Grk “at the ninth hour.” This is calculated from sunrise (Josephus, Ant. 14.4.3 [14.65]; Dan 9:21).
verses.commentary:
3:1 "Peter and John were going up to the temple" This is an IMPERFECT ACTIVE INDICATIVE.
It was the habit of all of the early disciples to go to the temple often (cf. Luke 24:53; Acts 2:46). The
original followers of Jesus in Palestine worshiped

- in the temple (at least on special days if not daily)

- in the local synagogue (every Sabbath)

- with believers on Sunday

This was the pattern for a long period of time. These believers saw no division between
their faith in Jesus as the Promised Messiah (see
SPECIAL TOPIC: MESSIAH) and Judaism. They saw themselves as the "people or
congregation of Israel." This is why they chose the name ekklesia for their group. In the
Septuagint this is how the Hebrew covenantal phrase, "the congregation (qahal) of Israel"
was translated (see
SPECIAL TOPIC: CHURCH).

The Pharisees (the only surviving sect of Judaism, see
SPECIAL TOPIC: PHARISEES) took official action after the fall of Jerusalem
and instituted an oath formula (i.e., the Eighteen Benedictions from the Reform of Judaism at Jamnia in the
A.D. 70-90, which specifically rejected Jesus as the Messiah) for the purpose of restricting
membership in the local synagogues. This is when the church solidified its day of worship as Sunday (the day to
commemorate Jesus' resurrection; the day Jesus appeared three times to the disciples in the Upper Room).

John is often identified with Peter in Acts (cf. Acts 1:13; 3:1,3,4,11; 4:13,19; 8:14). It
is surely possible that the early church in Jerusalem had groups of leaders which represented different
perspectives and emphases of the gospel.

- possibly Peter and John were more open to Gentile evangelism (cf. Acts 3:8,10)

- while James (the half-brother of Jesus) was more identified with a conservative Jewish element

- all this changed to some extent after the Jerusalem Council of Acts 15

▣ "at the ninth hour, the hour of prayer" This would denote nine hours after sunrise.
The Jews (i.e., Pharisees) had traditionally prayed each day at 9 a.m., 12 noon, and 3 p.m.
(possibly based on Ps. 55:17). This text refers to the time of the evening sacrifice, which was 3 p.m.
(the morning sacrifice was at 9 a.m.). Many people would have been in the temple at this time (i.e., "the continual").

verses.zh: 有一个人，生来是瘸腿的，天天被人抬来，放在殿的一个门口（那门名叫美门），要求进殿的人周济。
verses.en: And a man lame[NOTE:1] from birth[NOTE:2] was being carried up, who was placed at the temple gate called “the Beautiful Gate” every day[NOTE:3] so he could beg for money[NOTE:4] from those going into the temple courts.[NOTE:5]
notes: Or “crippled.”
Grk “from his mother’s womb.”
BDAG 437 s.v. ἡμέρα 2.c has “every day” for this phrase.

Grk “alms.” The term “alms” is not in common use today, so what the man expected, “money,” is used in the translation instead. The idea is that of money given as a gift to someone who was poor. Giving alms was viewed as honorable in Judaism (Tob 1:3, 16; 12:8-9; m. Pe’ah 1:1). See also Luke 11:41; 12:33; Acts 9:36; 10:2, 4, 31; 24:17.

Grk “the temple.” This is actually a reference to the courts surrounding the temple proper, and has been translated accordingly.sn Into the temple courts. The exact location of this incident is debated. The ‘Beautiful Gate’ referred either to the Nicanor Gate (which led from the Court of the Gentiles into the Court of Women) or the Shushan Gate at the eastern wall.
verses.commentary:
3:2 "a man who had been lame from his mother's womb" All of the regular attenders of the temple
knew of this man's condition ("was being carried repeatedly" is an IMPERFECT PASSIVE);
therefore, there was no chance of a trick being involved in the healing (cf. Acts 3:10; 4:22). This was a
fulfillment of OT Messianic prophecy (cf. Isa. 35:6). The Jews wanted a sign; Jesus gave them many,
now they have another if they only had spiritual eyes to see.

Here is the shocking paradox of the sick sitting daily at the house of God. As a
matter of fact, there was even a prohibition against these kinds of people actively participating
in worship, as well as serving as priests (cf. Lev. 21:16-24). The gospel offers a new day. Even an
Ethiopian (no race barriers) eunuch (no physical barriers) is welcome in the new kingdom (cf. Acts 8:26-40).

▣ "the gate of the temple which is called Beautiful" The exact location of this gate is
uncertain. It was possibly the Nicanor Gate which was made of Corinthian brass (Flavius Josephus,
Antiq. 15.11.3; Wars 5.5.3). It led from the Court of the Gentiles to the Court of
the Women. It was on the eastern side of the temple complex, facing the Mount of Olives, close to Solomon's Portico.

▣ "to beg alms of those who were entering" Almsgiving, or giving to the poor, was
a required part of the Jewish faith (cf. Matt. 6:1-4; Luke 11:41;
12:33; Acts 10:2,4,31; 24:17). Usually money was collected weekly in the local synagogues and
then food distributed, but apparently some begged daily in the temple area itself.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ALMSGIVING

verses.zh: 他看见彼得、约翰将要进殿，就求他们周济。
verses.en: When he saw Peter and John about to go into the temple courts,[NOTE:1] he asked them for money.[NOTE:2]
notes: Grk “the temple.” This is actually a reference to the courts surrounding the temple proper, and has been translated accordingly.sn See the note on the phrase the temple courts in the previous verse.
Grk “alms.” See the note on the word “money” in the previous verse.
verses.commentary: 3:3 The man's motive was originally only monetary (cf. Acts 3:5).

verses.zh: 彼得、约翰定睛看他；彼得说：「你看我们！」
verses.en: Peter looked directly[NOTE:1] at him (as did John) and said, “Look at us!”
notes: Grk “Peter, looking directly at him, as did John, said.” The participle ἀτενίσας (atenisas) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.
verses.commentary:
3:4 "fixed his gaze on" See note at Acts 1:10.

▣ "look at us" They wanted his undivided attention (blepō is in
an AORIST ACTIVE IMPERATIVE form).

verses.zh: 那人就留意看他们，指望得着甚么。
verses.en: So the lame man[NOTE:1] paid attention to them, expecting to receive something from them.
notes: Grk “So he”; the referent (the lame man) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
verses.commentary:
3:5 The Apostles were not monetarily wealthy men, but they had access to the spiritual
resources of God (cf. Acts 3:6).

verses.zh: 彼得说：「金银我都没有，只把我所有的给你：我奉拿撒勒人耶稣基督的名，叫你起来行走！」
verses.en: But Peter said, “I have no silver or gold,[NOTE:1] but what I do have I give you. In the name[NOTE:2] of Jesus Christ[NOTE:3] the Nazarene, stand up and[NOTE:4] walk!”
notes: Or “I have no money.” L&N 6.69 classifies the expression ἀργύριον καὶ χρυσίον (argurion kai chrusion) as an idiom that is a generic expression for currency, thus “money.”

In the name. Note the authority in the name of Jesus the Messiah. His presence and power are at work for the man. The reference to “the name” is not like a magical incantation, but is designed to indicate the agent who performs the healing. The theme is quite frequent in Acts (2:38 plus 21 other times).
Or “Messiah”; both “Christ” (Greek) and “Messiah” (Hebrew and Aramaic) mean “one who has been anointed.”

The words “stand up and” (ἔγειρε καί, egeire kai) are not in a few mss (א B D sa), but are included in A C E Ψ 095 33 1739 M lat sy mae bo. The external testimony is thus fairly evenly divided, with few but signficant representatives of the Alexandrian and Western textual clusters supporting the shorter reading. Internally, the words look like a standard scribal emendation, and may have been motivated by other healing passages where Jesus gave a similar double command (cf. Matt 9:5; Mark 2:9, [11]; Luke 5:23; [6:8]; John 5:8). On the other hand, there is some motivation for deleting ἔγειρε καί here, namely, unlike Jesus’ healing miracles, Peter raises (ἤγειρεν, ēgeiren) the man to his feet (v. 7) rather than the man rising on his own. In light of the scribal tendency to harmonize, especially in immediate context, the longer reading is slightly preferred.
verses.commentary:
3:6 "In the name of Jesus Christ" "Name" is a Hebrew idiom which speaks of one's character
(cf. Luke 9:48,49; 10:17; 21:12,17; 24:47). This must have been shocking to this man. Jesus was a
recently condemned and crucified criminal, whom this stranger (i.e,. Peter) was calling "the Messiah"
(i.e., "The Christ," which is the Greek translation).

SPECIAL TOPIC: The Name of the Lord

SPECIAL TOPIC: Christ Jesus As Lord

▣ "The Nazarene" This word has a Messianic connotation (i.e., "The Branch").

SPECIAL TOPIC: JESUS THE NAZARENE

▣ "walk" This is a PRESENT ACTIVE IMPERATIVE. Peter and John, like Jesus,
used a chance encounter to demonstrate God's love and power and also to confirm the gospel message
(cf. Acts 3:9). This healing drew the attention of the Jewish worshipers (cf. Acts 3:12ff).

The purpose of miracles was to

- get people's attention to hear and be open to the gospel message

- show the heart of God related to the suffering of fallen mankind

- show the validity and power of the person of Jesus the Messiah (i.e., in His name)

- continue to engage the Jewish leadership to the issue of Jesus as the true Messiah

verses.zh: 于是拉着他的右手，扶他起来；他的脚和踝子骨立刻健壮了，
verses.en: Then[NOTE:1] Peter[NOTE:2] took hold[NOTE:3] of him by the right hand and raised him up, and at once the man’s[NOTE:4] feet and ankles were made strong.[NOTE:5]
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “Then” to reflect the sequence of events.
Grk “he”; the referent (Peter) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Grk “Peter taking hold of him…raised him up.” The participle πιάσας (piasas) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.
Grk “his”; the referent (the man) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

At once the man’s feet and ankles were made strong. Note that despite the past lameness, the man is immediately able to walk. The restoration of his ability to walk pictures the presence of a renewed walk, a fresh start at life; this was far more than money would have given him.
verses.commentary:
3:7 This is an eyewitness account of several related events. Someone who was there told Luke
about this in vivid, detailed terms. Remember, Luke interviewed several people in his research for writing
a Gospel account.

▣ "feet and ankles" These terms are used only here in the NT. They are medical terms
used by Galen (i.e., famous physican, A.D. 129-216). They demonstrate Luke's medical orientation.
This is also true of the VERB "strengthened," v. 7, and "leap" in v. 8. See M. R. Vincent,
Word Studies in the New Testament, p. 229.

▣ "immediately" This is the Greek term parachrēma. Luke uses it ten times
in his Gospel and six times in Acts (cf. Acts 3:7; 5:10; 12:23; 13:11; 16:26,33). It is used only
twice in Matthew and nowhere else in the NT. It is used several times in the Septuagint. Luke uses
idioms and terms from this Greek translation of the Hebrew OT often. He must have known the OT well,
possibly from his contact with the Apostle Paul or involvement in Christian catechism with new believers.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SEPTUAGINT

verses.zh: 就跳起来，站着，又行走，同他们进了殿，走着，跳着，赞美　神。
verses.en: He[NOTE:1] jumped up,[NOTE:2] stood and began walking around, and he entered the temple courts[NOTE:3] with them, walking and leaping and praising God.
notes: Grk “And he.” Because of the length and complexity of the Greek sentence, the conjunction καί (kai) has not been translated here. Instead a new English sentence is begun.

Grk “Jumping up, he stood.” The participle ἐξαλλόμενος (exallomenos) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style. It is possible that the paralyzed man actually jumped off the ground, but more probably this term simply refers to the speed with which he stood up. See L&N 15.240.
Grk “the temple.” This is actually a reference to the courts surrounding the temple proper, and has been translated accordingly.
verses.commentary:
3:8 "With a leap he stood upright" This is a PRESENT MIDDLE PARTICIPLE (cf. Acts 3:9).
This man began walking all around this section of the temple complex. What an opportunity to share the Good News!

verses.zh: 百姓都看见他行走，赞美　神；
verses.en: All[NOTE:1] the people saw him walking and praising God,
notes: Grk “And all.” Because of the difference between Greek style, which often begins sentences or clauses with “and,” and English style, which generally does not, καί (kai) has not been translated here.

verses.zh: 认得他是那素常坐在殿的美门口求周济的，就因他所遇着的事满心希奇、惊讶。
verses.en: and they recognized him as the man who used to sit and ask for donations[NOTE:1] at the Beautiful Gate of the temple, and they were filled with astonishment and amazement[NOTE:2] at what had happened to him.
notes: Grk “alms,” but this term is not in common use today, so the closest modern equivalent, “donations,” is used instead. The idea is that of a donation to charity.

Amazement is a frequent response to miracles of Jesus or the apostles. These took the ancients by as much surprise as they would people today. But in terms of response to what God is doing, amazement does not equal faith (Luke 4:36; 5:9, 26; 7:16).
verses.commentary:
3:10 They knew this man (IMPERFECT ACTIVE INDICATIVE, they began to recognize him).
He was no stranger or visitor. They had seen him at the gate day after day, and passed by! However,
Jesus' representatives did not just pass by, they acted in Pentecostal power!

▣ "they were filled" Luke uses this term often (see full note at Acts 5:17). Humans
can be "filled" with many things (i.e., characterized by):

- the Holy Spirit, Luke 1:15,41,67; Acts 2:4; 4:8,31; 9:17; 13:9

- rage, Luke 4:28; 6:11

- fear, Luke 5:26

- wonder and amazement, Acts 3:10

- jealousy, Acts 5:17; 13:45

- confusion, Acts 19:29

Peter and John wanted these who were amazed (he got their attention) to be filled
with the gospel! See full note at Acts 5:17.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FILLED

▣ "wonder and amazement" These things are also common in Luke's writings.

- wonder

- thambos, Luke 3:6; 5:9; Acts 3:10

- ekthambos in Acts 3:11

- amazement

- ekstasis, Luke 5:26; Acts 3:10; 10:10; 11:5; 22:17

- existēmi, Luke 2:47; 8:56; 24:22; Acts 2:7,12; 8:9,11; 9:21; 10:45; 12:16

God's love and acts always cause amazement. These Greek words were used in the Septuagint
for fear and awe of God, cf. Gen. 15:12; Exod. 23:27; Deut. 28:28.

verses.zh: 那人正在称为所罗门的廊下，拉着彼得、约翰；众百姓一齐跑到他们那里，很觉希奇。
verses.en: While the man[NOTE:1] was hanging on to Peter and John, all the people, completely astounded, ran together to them in the covered walkway[NOTE:2] called Solomon’s Portico.[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “he”; the referent (the man) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

Or “portico,” “colonnade”; Grk “stoa.” The translation “covered walkway” (a descriptive translation) was used here because the architectural term “portico” or “colonnade” is less familiar. However, the more technical term “portico” was retained in the actual name that follows.

Solomon’s Portico was a covered walkway formed by rows of columns supporting a roof and open on the inner side facing the center of the temple complex. It was located on the east side of the temple (Josephus, Ant. 15.11.3-5 [15.391-420], 20.9.7 [20.221]) and was a place of commerce and conversation.
verses.commentary:
3:11 "while he was clinging to Peter" This is a PRESENT ACTIVE PARTICIPLE. I
would imagine he was holding on to Peter as Mary Magdalene held on to Jesus in the garden (cf. John 20:16-17).

▣ "the portico of Solomon" This was a long covered area along the eastern side of the
court of the Gentiles (cf. Josephus' Antiq. 20.9.7). The roof was supported by many columns.
It got its name from the fact that the old foundations of Solomon's temple were located in the same
general area. Jesus taught there often (cf. John 10:23).

verses.zh: 彼得看见，就对百姓说：「以色列人哪，为甚么把这事当作希奇呢？为甚么定睛看我们，以为我们凭自己的能力和虔诚使这人行走呢？
verses.en: When Peter saw this, he declared to the people, “Men of Israel,[NOTE:1] why are you amazed at this? Why[NOTE:2] do you stare at us as if we had made this man[NOTE:3] walk by our own power or piety?
notes: Or perhaps “People of Israel,” since this was taking place in Solomon’s Portico and women may have been present. The Greek ἄνδρες ᾿Ισραηλῖται (andres Israēlitai) used in the plural would normally mean “men, gentlemen” (BDAG 79 s.v. ἀνήρ 1.a).
Grk “or why.”
Grk “him”; the referent (the man) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
verses.commentary:
3:12 "when Peter saw this" They saw the amazement and curiosity of the crowd and
took advantage (cf. Col. 4:3; 2 Tim. 4:2) of the opportunity to share the gospel (i.e., the second recorded
sermon of the new church).

▣ "Men of Israel" Peter also called them this in Acts 2:22. Peter is still addressing Jews.

SPECIAL TOPIC: JEWS

SPECIAL TOPIC: ISRAEL (the name)

▣ "why. . .why" Peter asked why they were surprised by a miraculous healing. Had not
Jesus performed these kinds of miracles especially during the last week of His life?

Also, why did they look at Peter and John so admiringly, as if they did it? This was
a sign of the trustworthiness of the gospel and the power of the name of the resurrected Messiah.

The Spirit performed this miracle for several reasons.

- to confirm the leadership of Peter and John

- to help a needy man

- to witness to the Jews at the temple

verses.zh: 亚伯拉罕、以撒、雅各的　神，就是我们列祖的　神，已经荣耀了他的仆人（或译：儿子）耶稣；你们却把他交付彼拉多。彼拉多定意要释放他，你们竟在彼拉多面前弃绝了他。
verses.en: The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob,[NOTE:1] the God of our forefathers,[NOTE:2] has glorified[NOTE:3] his servant[NOTE:4] Jesus, whom you handed over and rejected[NOTE:5] in the presence of Pilate after he had decided[NOTE:6] to release him.
notes: ‡ The repetition of ὁ θεός (ho theos, “God”) before the names of Isaac and Jacob is found in P74 א C (A D without article) 36 104 1175 lat. The omission of the second and third ὁ θεός is supported by B E Ψ 33 1739 M. The other time that Exod 3:6 is quoted in Acts (7:32) the best witnesses also lack the repeated ὁ θεός, but the three other times this OT passage is quoted in the NT the full form, with the thrice-mentioned θεός, is used (Matt 22:32; Mark 12:26; Luke 20:37). Scribes would be prone to conform the wording here to the LXX; the longer reading is thus most likely not authentic. NA28 has the words in brackets, indicating doubts as to their authenticity.

Or “ancestors”; Grk “fathers.”sn The reference to the God of the patriarchs is a reminder that God is the God of the nation and of promises. The phrase God of our forefathers is from the Hebrew scriptures (Exod 3:6, 15-16; 4:5; see also the Jewish prayer known as “The Eighteen Benedictions”). Once again, event has led to explanation, or what is called the “sign and speech” pattern.
Has glorified. Jesus is alive, raised and active, as the healing illustrates so dramatically how God honors him.
His servant. The term servant has messianic connotations given the context of the promise, the note of suffering, and the titles and functions noted in vv. 14-15.
Or “denied,” “disowned.”
This genitive absolute construction could be understood as temporal (“when he had decided”) or concessive (“although he had decided”).
verses.commentary:
3:13 "The God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob" This shows that Jesus' ministry and the gospel were
vitally connected to the Covenant God and Covenant people of the Old Testament (cf. Exod. 3:6,15; Luke 20:37).

Christianity must be characterized as the true fulfillment of Judaism (cf. Matt. 5:17-19).
Many Jews would see it as a perversion, but NT writers saw it as a fulfillment. The followers of Jesus
are the promised fruition of the "new covenant" of Jer. 31:31-34 (cf. Gal. 6:16). Israel did not complete
her missionary task of being a kingdom of priests for the world (cf. Exod. 19:5-6; 1 Pet. 2:5,9; Rev. 1:6).
The church has been given the mandate (cf. Matt. 28:18-20; Luke 24:46-47; Acts 1:8). God's goal is the
restoration of His image in mankind, so that His initial purpose of fellowship can be accomplished. If
there is only one God (i.e., monotheism), then there cannot be a special people, only servants to serve
God's universal purposes with all humanity.

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS

SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM

SPECIAL TOPIC: WHY ARE OT COVENANT PROMISES SO DIFFERENT FROM NT COVENANT PROMISES?

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣ "has glorified" This term can be understood in several ways.

- the immediate context to the healing of the lame man in Jesus' name

- the larger context of Peter's sermon about Jesus being resurrected and thereby glorified

- the OT texts about Jesus as the coming Messiah (cf. Luke 24:26-27)

- in John's Gospel this term is always used by Jesus Himself for His crucifixion
(cf. Acts 7:39; 12:10,23; 13:31-32; 16:14; 17:1)

SPECIAL TOPIC: GLORY (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: GLORY (NT)

▣ "His servant" The term "servant" (pais used regularly in the LXX)

- an honorific title in the OT for God's called leaders used for Jacob, Moses, Joshua, and David (cf. Psalm 105; Luke 1:69)

- in the Servant Songs of Isaiah for the Messiah (i.e., Isa. 42:1-5; 49:1-7; 50:4-11; 52:13-53:12)

- the nation of Israel (cf. Isa. 41:8-9; 42:19; 43:10; 44:1,21; also LXX seen in Luke 1:54)

- God's Messiah (cf. Isa. 42:1; 52:13; 53:11)

- Pais is used of Jesus as the Servant/Messiah in Acts 3:13,26; 4:27,30

There is not a clear distinction between the corporate and individual aspect, especially
in the last Servant Song (i.e., Isa. 52:13-53:12). In Isa. 52:13-53:12 it cannot refer to Israel because

- the nation cannot be the innocent one who brings redemption because the nation deserves
the judgment (cf. Isa. 41:18-22; 53:8d)

- the Septuagint changes "you" in Isa. 52:14 to "Him" (also in Acts 3:15). The Jewish
translators of the LXX before Jesus' birth (possibly 250-150 B.C.) saw this text as
Messianic and individual.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MY SERVANT

▣ "Jesus" When the name Jesus is used by itself, it usually emphasizes His humanness
(cf. Acts 3:6).

▣ "whom you delivered and disowned" The "you" (PLURAL) is emphatic! It was not only the Jewish
leaders who were responsible for Jesus' death (cf. Acts 3:17; 2:23). Peter makes a specific reference
to the crowd's responses before Pilate (cf. Luke 23:18-25). It is possible some of these may have
been there, but Peter addresses this crowd as if they were responsible as a group (cf. Acts 3:15).
God's chosen people (Israelites/Jews) "delivered up" and "disowned" God's Messiah (cf. John 1:11).

▣ "Pilate" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: PONTIUS PILATE

▣ "when he had decided to release Him" This refers to Luke 23:4,14,22, where Pilate
says three times, "I find no guilt in Him," as well as the three times he tried to release Him
(cf. Luke 23:16,20,22). Many scholars believe Acts was written to show that Roman officials did
not find Jesus treasonous. Pilate was forced by the Jewish leadership to do that which he was
reluctant to do himself. Christianity was not a threat to Rome.

verses.zh: 你们弃绝了那圣洁公义者，反求着释放一个凶手给你们。
verses.en: But you rejected[NOTE:1] the Holy and Righteous One and asked that a man who was a murderer be released to you.
notes: Or “denied,” “disowned.”
verses.commentary:
3:14 "the Holy and Righteous One" This states clearly the innocence and sinlessness of Jesus.
The trial was a farce. This is another OT Messianic title.

- "The Holy One"

- Peter ‒ John 6:69

- demons ‒ Mark 1:24; Luke 4:34

- "The Righteous One" ‒ Isa. 53:11; Acts 7:52; 22:14

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE HOLY ONE

SPECIAL TOPIC: RIGHTEOUSNESS

▣ "and asked for a murderer" It is so ironic that Barabbas was guilty of the exact crime
they accused Jesus of-sedition (cf. Luke 23:18-19,23-25).

verses.zh: 你们杀了那生命的主，　神却叫他从死里复活了；我们都是为这事作见证。
verses.en: You killed[NOTE:1] the Originator[NOTE:2] of life, whom God raised[NOTE:3] from the dead. To this fact we are witnesses![NOTE:4]
notes: Or “You put to death.”
Or “Founder,” “founding Leader.”
Whom God raised. God is the main actor here, as he testifies to Jesus and vindicates him.

We are witnesses. Note the two witnesses here, Peter and John (Acts 5:32; Heb 2:3-4).tn Grk “whom God raised from the dead, of which we are witnesses.” The two consecutive relative clauses make for awkward English style, so the second was begun as a new sentence with the words “to this fact” supplied in place of the Greek relative pronoun to make a complete sentence in English.
verses.commentary:
3:15 "but put to death" It is surprising that in the many texts which mention Jesus' death
in Acts (cf. Acts 2:23,36; 3:15; 4:10; 5:30; 7:52; 10:39; 13:28) very little is developed along
the lines of Gen. 3:15 or Isaiah 53.

There is also variety in how His death is phrased.

- nailed to a cross - Acts 2:23

- crucified - Acts 2:36; 4:10

- put to death - Acts 3:15; 13:28

- put to death by hanging Him on a cross - Acts 5:30; 10:39

- killed - Acts 7:52

His death and resurrection are emphasized but not His substitutionary atonement (i.e., Mark 10:45;
John 1:29; 2 Cor. 5:21).

NASB, NKJV, NJB, Peshitta, REB
"the Prince of life"

NKJV, NIV
"the Author of life"

TEV
"the one who leads to life"

Moffatt
"the pioneer of life"

See full discussion of the title in the Special Topic below. The term is an obvious
contrast to "murderer" (Acts 3:14).

SPECIAL TOPIC: AUTHOR/LEADER (archēgos)

▣ "God raised from the dead" Usually in the NT it is the Father who raises the Son from
the dead as a sign of His approval of Jesus' life, teachings, and substitutionary death. The NT also
affirms that all three persons of the Trinity were active in Jesus' resurrection:

- the Spirit (cf. Rom. 8:11)

- the Son (cf. John 2:19-22; 10:17-18)

- the Father (cf. Acts 2:24,32; 3:15,26; 4:10; 5:30; 10:40; 13:30,33,34,37; 17:31; Rom. 6:4,9)

This is a major theological aspect of the Kerygma. If this is not true, all else
is not true (cf. 1 Cor. 15:12-19).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE TRINITY

SPECIAL TOPIC: RESURRECTION

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE KERYGMA
OF THE EARLY CHURCH

▣ "a fact to which we are witnesses" This is either

- an emphasis on primary source material; these hearers were eyewitnesses of the events of the
last week of Jesus' life in Jerusalem (cf. Acts 2:22)

- a reference to the Apostles and disciples in the Upper Room (cf. Acts 1:22; 2:32)

In context number 2 seems best.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WITNESSES TO JESUS

verses.zh: 我们因信他的名，他的名便叫你们所看见所认识的这人健壮了；正是他所赐的信心，叫这人在你们众人面前全然好了。
verses.en: And on the basis of faith in Jesus’[NOTE:1] name,[NOTE:2] his very name has made this man—whom you see and know—strong. The[NOTE:3] faith that is through Jesus[NOTE:4] has given him this complete health in the presence[NOTE:5] of you all.
notes: Grk “in his name”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Here is another example of appeal to the person by mentioning the name. See the note on the word name in 3:6.
Grk “see and know, and the faith.” Because of the length and complexity of the Greek sentence, a new sentence was started here in the translation and καί (kai, “and”) has not been translated.

The faith that is through Jesus. Note how this verse explains how the claim to “faith in Jesus’ name” works and what it means. To appeal to the name is to point to the person. It is not clear that the man expressed faith before the miracle. This could well be a “grace-faith miracle” where God grants power through the apostles to picture how much a gift life is (Luke 17:11-19). Christology and grace are emphasized here.tn Grk “him”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Or “in full view.”
verses.commentary:
3:16 "on the basis of faith" This same phrase occurs in Phil. 3:9 (both have the
ARTICLE with "faith"). The Greek term "faith"
(pistis) can be translated into English as "faith," "trust," or "believe." It is humanity's
conditional response to God's unconditional grace (cf. Eph. 2:8-9). It is basically the believer's
trusting in the trustworthiness of God (i.e., His character, His promises, His Messiah) or faithing
God's faithfulness!

It is difficult in the healing accounts of the Gospels and Acts to document
the spiritual (i.e., covenantal) side of the event. Those healed are not
always "saved" (cf. John 5). Personal faith is not always present in
healing accounts. Sometimes they were done for a witness to others in order to engender faith.

The Greek PREPOSITION used in this phrase, eis (cf. Phil. 3:9), is
rare when used of one's faith in Christ (similar expression in Acts 2:38). Usually one of several
PREPOSITIONS is used.

- by Paul

- dia - Rom. 3:22,25,30; Gal. 2:16; 3:14,26; Eph. 2:8; 3:12,17; Col. 2:12; 2 Tim. 3:15; 1 Pet. 1:5

- ek - Rom. 9:30; 14:23; Gal. 3:8,9,22; 5:5; James 2:24

- en -1 Cor. 16:13; 2 Cor. 13:5; Gal. 2:20; 1 Tim. 3:13

- both eis and ek are used in Rom. 1:17

- by John (see
SPECIAL TOPIC: John's Use of the VERB Believe)

There was no standardized phrase to express "saving faith."

SPECIAL TOPIC: JOHN'S USE OF THE VERB "BELIEVE"

- a. "the name of Jesus" (see

b. "has strengthened this man"

c. "whom you see and know

b. "has given him this perfect health"

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEALING

verses.zh: 弟兄们，我晓得你们做这事是出于不知，你们的官长也是如此。
verses.en: And now, brothers, I know you acted in ignorance,[NOTE:1] as your rulers did too.
notes: The ignorance Peter mentions here does not excuse them from culpability. It was simply a way to say “you did not realize the great mistake you made.”
verses.commentary:
3:17 "I know that you acted in ignorance" This reflects Jesus' words from the cross
(cf. Luke 23:34). However, even in their ignorance, the people were still spiritually responsible!
In some ways this excuse was a way to help people accept their own responsibility (cf. Acts 13:27;
17:30; 26:9; 1 Cor. 2:8). For a good discussion see Millard Erickson,
Christian Theology, 2nd ed., pp. 583-585.

▣ "just as your rulers did also" Luke often makes a distinction between the people
and their rulers (cf. Luke 7:29-30; 23:35; Acts 13:27; 14:5). The real issue in trying to do this
may be the mutual responsibility of both groups. Often it is asserted that Jesus does not condemn
Jews as a whole, but their illegal (i.e., not of Aaronic descent) leaders. It is surely difficult
to know if the cursing of the fig tree (cf. Mark 11:12-14,20-24) and the parable of the unjust
vineyard tenants (cf. Luke 20:9-18) are condemnations of Judaism of the first century or only
its leaders. Luke asserts it is both!

verses.zh: 但神曾藉众先知的口，预言基督将要受害，就这样应验了。
verses.en: But the things God foretold[NOTE:1] long ago through[NOTE:2] all the prophets—that his Christ[NOTE:3] would suffer—he has fulfilled in this way.
notes: God foretold. Peter’s topic is the working out of God’s plan and promise through events the scriptures also note.
Grk “by the mouth of” (an idiom).
Or “Messiah”; both “Christ” (Greek) and “Messiah” (Hebrew and Aramaic) mean “one who has been anointed.”sn See the note on Christ in 2:31.
verses.commentary:
3:18 "announced beforehand" The gospel was no afterthought with God, but His eternal,
purposeful plan (cf. Gen. 3:15; Mark 10:45; Luke 22:22; Acts 2:23; 3:18; 4:28; Rom. 1:2; see

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN). The
early sermons in Acts (the kerygma) present Jesus as the fulfillment of OT promises and prophecies.

There are several aspects of the Kerygma (i.e., the major theological
aspects of the sermons in Acts) expressed in these verses.

- faith in Jesus is essential

- Jesus' person and work were prophesied by OT prophets

- the Messiah must suffer

- they must repent

- Jesus is coming again

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE KERYGMA OF THE EARLY CHURCH

▣ "by the mouth of all the prophets" Jesus fulfilled OT prophecy
(cf. Acts 3:34, Matt. 5:17-48). I think Jesus Himself showed the two on the road to Emmaus
(cf. Luke 24:13-35) the OT prophecies that pertained to His suffering, death, and resurrection. They
shared this with the Apostles, who made it part of their preaching (cf. Luke 24:45).

This imagery, "through the mouth of. . ." is a characteristic way of Luke's (cf. Acts
1:16; 3:18,21; 4:25; Luke 1:70) asserting the inspiration of the Bible. The Spirit spoke through human
vessels to record divine revelation (i.e., 2 Tim. 3:16).

SPECIAL TOPIC: INSPIRATION

▣ "Christ" This is the Greek translation of the Hebrew/Aramaic word " Messiah," which means
Anointed One. This refers to God's special agent whose life and death would inaugurate the New Age of
righteousness, the New Age of the Spirit.

The affirmation that Jesus was/is the Christ/Messiah promised by YHWH becomes a
recurrent theme of the preaching of Acts.

- Peter - 2:31; 3:18; Acts 5:42; 8:5

- Paul - 9:22; 17:3; Acts 18:5,28

SPECIAL TOPIC: MESSIAH

SPECIAL TOPIC: "ANOINTING" IN THE BIBLE

▣ "suffer" This was alluded to in several OT texts (cf. Gen. 3:15; Psalm 22; Isaiah 53;
Zech. 12:10). This aspect of a suffering Messiah is what surprised the Jews (cf. 1 Cor. 1:23). They
were expecting a conquering general (i.e., like the Judges in the OT; cf. Rev. 20:11-16). This suffering Messiah
was a recurrent theme of Apostolic sermons in Acts

- Paul (cf. Acts 17:3; 26:23)

- Peter (cf. Acts 3:18; 1 Pet. 1:10-12; 2:21; 3:18)

SPECIAL TOPIC: A SUFFERING MESSIAH

verses.zh: 所以，你们当悔改归正，使你们的罪得以涂抹，
verses.en: Therefore repent and turn back so that your sins may be wiped out,
verses.commentary:
3:19 "repent and return" The Greek term "repent" means a change of mind. This is
an AORIST ACTIVE IMPERATIVE of metanoeō. The Hebrew term for repentance
means "change of action" ("return" [emistrephō] may reflect the Hebrew "turn" shub,
cf. Num. 10:36; Deut. 30:2,10) in the Septuagint. Repentance is a necessary covenant item in
salvation along with faith (cf. Mark 1:15 and Acts 3:16,19; 20:21). Acts mentions it often
(cf. Peter - 2:38; 3:19,26 and Paul - 14:15; 17:30; 20:21; 26:20). Repentance is
indispensable (cf. Luke 13:3 and 2 Peter 3:9). It is basically a willingness to change. It is a
both a human volitional act and a gift of God (cf. Acts 5:31; 11:18; 2 Tim. 2:25). Repentance is "a turning
from," while faith is "a turning to"!

This gospel invitation (vv. 17-26) is parallel to Acts 2:37-38. But notice there is no mention
of baptism. Here, repentance is the crucial element.

SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (NT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: EASTERN LITERATURE
(biblical paradoxes)

▣ "sins may be wiped away" This term means "to erase"; "blot out"; or "wipe away"
(cf. Col. 2:14; Rev. 3:5; 7:17; 21:4). What a promise! In the ancient world ink was acid and was,
therefore, impossible to erase. This is a true miracle of God's grace (cf. Ps. 51:1; 103:11-13;
Isa. 1:18; 38:17; 43:25; 44:22; Jer. 31:34; Micah 7:19). When God forgives, God forgets (erases)!

▣ "times of refreshing" The Greek term (anapsuchō, anapsuxis) basically
means "breathing space, relaxation, relief" (Baker, Arndt, Gingrich, and Danker, A Greek-English
Lexicon, p. 63), "refresh by air," or "treat a wound with air" (Kittle, Theological Dictionary
of the New Testament, vol. 9, p. 663). The metaphorical extension is physical or spiritual
refreshment or restoration.

In the Septuagint it is used of regaining physical strength after a battle
(cf. Exod. 23:12; Jdgs. 15:19; 2 Sam. 16:14) or emotional refreshment as in 1 Sam. 16:23.

Peter's reference seems to be to an OT promise, but this phrase is not used in the OT.
For desert people's

- expanse was identified with freedom and joy

- while closed in spaces were a sign of distress and trouble

God was going to bring a widening, refreshing period of spiritual activity. This
Messianic activity had come in the gospel. The "times of refreshing" had come in Jesus of Nazareth.
However, the coming consummation would bring the New Age of the Spirit. In this specific context Peter
is referring to the Second Coming (cf. Acts 1:11). This phrase seems to be parallel to "the period of restoration"
(Acts 3:21).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE SECOND COMING (terms)

verses.zh: 这样，那安舒的日子就必从主面前来到；主也必差遣所预定给你们的基督（耶稣）降临。
verses.en: so that times of refreshing[NOTE:1] may come from the presence of the Lord,[NOTE:2] and so that he may send the Messiah[NOTE:3] appointed[NOTE:4] for you—that is, Jesus.
notes: Or “relief.”sn Times of refreshing. The phrase implies relief from difficult, distressful or burdensome circumstances. It is generally regarded as a reference to the messianic age being ushered in.

The words “so that…Lord” are traditionally placed in v. 19 by most English translations, but in the present translation the verse division follows the standard critical editions of the Greek text (NA28, UBS5).

He may send the Messiah appointed for you—that is, Jesus. The language points to the expectation of Jesus’ return to gather his people. It is a development of the question raised in Acts 1:6.tn Or “the Christ”; both “Christ” (Greek) and “Messiah” (Hebrew and Aramaic) mean “one who has been anointed.”
Or “designated in advance.”
verses.commentary:
3:20 "He may send Jesus" This is an AORIST ACTIVE SUBJUNCTIVE, which denotes
an element of contingency. The actions of Peter's hearers, in some sense, determined the time when YHWH will
send spiritual consummation (cf. F. F. Bruce, Answers to Questions, where he links Acts 3:19-21
with Rom. 11:25-27, p. 201).

The juxtaposition of "Jesus" next to "the Christ/the Messiah" seems to imply that
Peter is specifically asserting the Messiahship of Jesus of Nazareth. Later in the NT, "Lord,"
"Jesus," and "Christ" occur often, more as a combined referent to Jesus (i.e., the Lord Jesus Christ)
than an emphasis on the title Messiah. This is especially true in predominately Gentile churches.

SPECIAL TOPIC: Christ Jesus As Lord

▣ "the Christ appointed for you" This VERB is a PERFECT PASSIVE
PARTICIPLE. This same term is used of God's fore-choice in Acts 10:41; 22:14; 26:16; Jesus'
coming and dying has always been God's eternal redemptive plan (cf. Luke 22:22; Acts 2:23; 3:18; 4:28; 13:29; see

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN).

In the Septuagint this term reflects a choice, but without the foreknowledge (i.e.,
for Luke "pro" means before, cf. Exod. 4:13 and Josh. 3:12), which is obvious in this word's usage in
Acts. It does convey that sending Jesus was God's choice of blessing and redemption!

verses.zh: 天必留他，等到万物复兴的时候，就是　神从创世以来、藉着圣先知的口所说的。
verses.en: This one[NOTE:1] heaven must[NOTE:2] receive until the time all things are restored,[NOTE:3] which God declared[NOTE:4] from times long ago[NOTE:5] through his holy prophets.
notes: Grk “whom,” continuing the sentence from v. 20.
The term must used here (δεῖ, dei, “it is necessary”) is a key Lukan term to point to the plan of God and what must occur.

The time all things are restored. What that restoration involves is already recorded in the scriptures of the nation of Israel.tn Grk “until the times of the restoration of all things.” Because of the awkward English style of the extended genitive construction, and because the following relative clause has as its referent the “time of restoration” rather than “all things,” the phrase was translated “until the time all things are restored.”
Or “spoke.”
Or “from all ages past.”sn From times long ago. Once again, God’s plan is emphasized.
verses.commentary:
3:21

NASB, NKJV, Peshitta
"whom heaven must receive"

NRSV
"who must remain in heaven"

TEV, NIV
"He must remain in heaven"

NJB
"whom heaven must keep"

The SUBJECT of this phrase is "heaven"; the OBJECT is
"whom" (i.e., Jesus). There are two VERBALS in this phrase. The first is dei,
from deō, which means "it is necessary" or "it is proper." See full note at Acts 1:16. Here, it is used of
YHWH's plan for restoration of His creation into fellowship with Himself.

The second is an AORIST MIDDLE (deponent) INFINITIVE
of dechomai. Harold K Moulton, The Analytical Greek Lexicon Revised says in this
context it means "to receive into and retain" (p. 88). You can see how the English translations
pick up on the contextual aspect. Luke uses this term more than any other NT writer (13 times
in Luke and 8 times in Acts). Words must be defined in light of contextual usage and implication,
not etymology. Lexicons (dictionaries) only denote usage. They do not set definition!

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE ASCENSION

NASB
"until"

NKJV, NRSV, TEV, Peshitta, REB
"until"

NJB
"til"

This word is in the Greek UBS4 text. I do not know why NASB, 1995 edition,
put it in italics, which is the way to show it is not in the Greek text, but supplied for English
readers to understand.

In the 1970 edition of NASB, the "the" is in italics and not "until," which is correct.

▣ "period of restoration of all things" This refers to recreation (cf. Matt. 17:11; and
especially Rom. 8:13-23). The evil of human rebellion in Genesis 3 is nullified and creation is
restored; fellowship with God is reestablished. The image of God in mankind, damaged in the fall, has been
restored. Fellowship between God and humanity is restored. The initial purpose of creation is finally fulfilled.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND

▣ "about which God spoke by mouth of His holy prophets from ancient times" Mark's Gospel
begins with a quote from Mal. 3:1. Matthew 1:22-23 refers to the prophecy of Isa. 7:14. Luke used this
same phrase in Luke 1:70. One aspect of the Kerygma (i.e., recurrent theological truths in the
sermons in Acts) is that Jesus' birth, life, death, and resurrection fulfilled OT prophecy
(cf. Matt. 5:17-19; Luke 24:26-27). Jesus' ministry was not an afterthought or Plan B. It was the predetermined
plan of God (cf. Luke 22:22; Acts 2:23; 3:18; 4:28; 13:29). All things are working out to the fulfillment of
the total restoration of God's will for creation.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE KERYGMA OF THE EARLY CHURCH

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

verses.zh: 摩西曾说：『主―　神要从你们弟兄中间给你们兴起一位先知像我，凡他向你们所说的，你们都要听从。
verses.en: Moses said, ‘The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. You must obey[NOTE:1] him in everything he tells you.[NOTE:2]
notes: Grk “hear,” but the idea of “hear and obey” or simply “obey” is frequently contained in the Greek verb ἀκούω (akouō; see L&N 36.14) and the following context (v. 23) makes it clear that failure to “obey” the words of this “prophet like Moses” will result in complete destruction.
A quotation from Deut 18:15. By quoting Deut 18:15 Peter declared that Jesus was the eschatological “prophet like [Moses]” mentioned in that passage, who reveals the plan of God and the way of God.
verses.commentary:
3:22 "Moses said" The title "The Prophet" was used of the coming Messiah (cf. Deut. 18:14-22;
esp. 15,18; John 1:21,25). This documentation of Jesus from the Law of Moses (i.e., the most
authoritative part of the OT canon for Jews, both Sadducees and Pharisees) would have been very
important to these Jewish hearers. Jesus has always been God's plan of redemption (i.e., Gen. 3:15).
He came to die (cf. Mark 10:45; 2 Cor. 5:21).

SPECIAL TOPIC: JESUS IS GREATER THAN

SPECIAL TOPIC: MOSES' AUTHORSHIP OF THE PENTATEUCH

▣ "you shall give heed to everything He says to you" This use of the word "hear" denotes
the Hebrew VERB shema, which meant "to hear so as to do" (cf. Deut. 6:4).
Obedience is crucial (i.e., Luke 6:46). Disobedience brings destruction!

SPECIAL TOPIC: SHEMA (listen/hear)

SPECIAL TOPIC: KEEP

verses.zh: 凡不听从那先知的，必要从民中全然灭绝。』
verses.en: Every person[NOTE:1] who does not obey that prophet will be destroyed and thus removed[NOTE:2] from the people.’[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “every soul” (here “soul” is an idiom for the whole person).
Or “will be completely destroyed.” In Acts 3:23 the verb ἐξολεθρεύω (exolethreuō) is translated “destroy and remove” by L&N 20.35.
A quotation from Deut 18:19, also Lev 23:29. The OT context of Lev 23:29 discusses what happened when one failed to honor atonement. One ignored the required sacrifice of God at one’s peril.
verses.commentary:
3:23 This was a serious word of warning. It is an allusion to Deut. 18:19. Rejection of Jesus
was, and still is, a serious, eternal matter.

This allusion to Deut. 18:14-22 also has some significant theological insights.

- Notice both the individual and corporate aspects. Each individual soul must personally respond
to the Messiah. It is not enough to be a part of the corporate body of Israel.

- The phrase "utterly destroyed" is an allusion to "holy war." God will prune His own vine
(i.e., Israel, cf. John 15; Romans 9-11). Those who reject "the Prophet" are rejected by God.
The issue of salvation is one's faith response to God's Messiah.
Family, race, ethics, and meticulous performance of rules are not the New Covenant criteria
of salvation (i.e., Eph. 2:8-9), but faith in Christ (cf. 1 John 5:1-12).

verses.zh: 从撒母耳以来的众先知，凡说预言的，也都说到这些日子。
verses.en: And all the prophets, from Samuel and those who followed him, have spoken about and announced[NOTE:1] these days.
notes: Or “proclaimed.”sn All the prophets…have spoken about and announced. What Peter preaches is rooted in basic biblical and Jewish hope as expressed in the OT scriptures.
verses.commentary:
3:24 "Samuel" In the Jewish canon he (i.e., 1 Samuel) is considered one of the "Former Prophets,"
a part of the second division of the Hebrew canon. Samuel was called a prophet in 1 Sam. 3:20 and also
a seer (i.e., another term for prophet) in 1 Sam. 9:9; 1 Chr. 29:29.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW CANON

SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHET (different Hebrew terms)

▣ "these days" The "time of refreshing" (Acts 3:20) and "the period of restoration of
all things" (Acts 3:21) refer to the consummation of the Kingdom of God at the return of Christ, but
this phrase refers to the inauguration of the Messianic Kingdom, which occurred at the incarnation
of Jesus at Bethlehem or at least to the whole period of the latter days, which is the time between
Christ's two appearances on planet earth. The OT primarily understood only one coming of the Messiah.
His first coming as the "Suffering Servant" (Acts 3:18) was a surprise; His glorious return as
military leader and judge was expected.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE KINGDOM OF GOD

SPECIAL TOPIC: THIS AGE AND THE AGE TO COME

verses.zh: 你们是先知的子孙，也承受　神与你们祖宗所立的约，就是对亚伯拉罕说：『地上万族都要因你的后裔得福。』
verses.en: You are the sons of the prophets and of the covenant that God made with your ancestors,[NOTE:1] saying to Abraham, ‘And in your descendants[NOTE:2] all the nations[NOTE:3] of the earth will be blessed.’[NOTE:4]
notes: Or “forefathers”; Grk “fathers.”

Or “in your offspring”; Grk “in your seed.”sn In your descendants (Grk “in your seed”). Seed has an important ambiguity in this verse. The blessing comes from the servant (v. 26), who in turn blesses the responsive children of the covenant as the scripture promised. Jesus is the seed who blesses the seed.

Or “families.” The Greek word πατριά (patria) can indicate persons of succeeding generations who are related by birth (“lineage,” “family”) but it can also indicate a relatively large unit of people who make up a sociopolitical group and who share a presumed biological descent. In many contexts πατριά is very similar to ἔθνος (ethnos) and λαός (laos). In light of the context of the OT quotation, it is better to translate πατριά as “nations” here.
A quotation from Gen 22:18.
verses.commentary:
3:25 Peter addresses these Jews as the children of Abraham, the covenant people. However,
these covenant people must respond in faith and repentance to Jesus and the gospel or they will
be rejected (Acts 3:23)!

The NT (new covenant) is focused in a person, not a racial group. In the very call
of Abram there was a universal element (cf. Gen. 12:3). The universal offer has come in Christ and
is available to all (i.e., Luke wrote primarily to Gentiles. His Gospel and Acts made this
invitation repeatedly and specifically).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE GOSPEL

▣ "sons of" See

SPECIAL TOPIC: "SONS OF. . ." (OT)

▣ "covenant" This specifically refers to YHWH's covenant with the Patriarchs.

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS

▣ "all the families of the earth shall be blessed" This is an
allusion to God's promise to Abraham in Gen. 12:1-3. Notice the universal element in this quote from Gen. 22:18.
God chose Abraham to choose a people, to choose the world ( cf. Gen. 3:15; Exod. 19:5-6; Eph. 2:11-3:13).

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

verses.zh: 神既兴起他的仆人（或译：儿子），就先差他到你们这里来，赐福给你们，叫你们各人回转，离开罪恶。」
verses.en: God raised up[NOTE:1] his servant and sent him first to you, to bless you by turning[NOTE:2] each one of you from your iniquities.”[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “God raising up his servant, sent him.” The participle ἀναστήσας (anastēsas) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style. Some translations (e.g., NIV, NRSV) render this participle as temporal (“when God raised up his servant”).

The picture of turning is again seen as the appropriate response to the message. See v. 19 above. In v. 19 it was “turning to,” here it is “turning away from.” The direction of the two metaphors is important.

For the translation of plural πονηρία (ponēria) as “iniquities,” see G. Harder, TDNT 6:565. The plural is important, since for Luke turning to Jesus means turning away from sins, not just the sin of rejecting Jesus.
verses.commentary:
3:26 "For you first" The Jews, because of their Covenant heritage, have the first opportunity
to hear and understand the message of the gospel (cf. Rom. 1:16; 9:5). However, they must respond
in the same way as everyone else: repentance, faith, baptism, obedience, and perseverance.

▣ "raised up His Servant and sent Him" See note at Acts 2:24 and 3:13.

SPECIAL TOPIC: RESURRECTION

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS TO ACTS 3

In Acts 3-5 there is tension in Jerusalem over Jesus' teaching and the Apostle's miracles. The time frame
for the first five chapters is about one year.

- Peter and John heal the lame man, Acts 3:1-4:31 ( an example of Acts 2:43)

- the healing itself

- Peter's second sermon explaining the healing

- the reaction and trial (Peter's third sermon, given to the Sanhedrin)

- the persecution begins

- An attempt at communal life, Acts 4:32-5:11

- the early unity of believers (an example of Acts 2:43-47)

- the problems with Ananias and Sapphira

- The early church's relations with rabbinical Judaism, Acts 5:12-42

- the life of the church

- the jealousy of the Sanhedrin

- the intercession of an angel

- Peter's fourth sermon

- the reaction and punishment

TITLES FOR JESUS IN CHAPTERS 3-4

- Jesus Christ the Nazarene, Acts 3:6; 4:10

- His Servant Jesus, Acts 3:13,26; 4:27

- The Holy and Righteous One, 3:14 (cf. Acts 2:27)

- The Prince of Life, Acts 3:15

- The Christ, Acts 3:18,20; 4:10 (cf. "Lord and Christ," Acts 2:36)

- Prophet, Acts 3:22

- Possibly an allusion to the title "Seed of Abraham," Acts 3:25-26

- The Cornerstone, Acts 4:11
